source.title: LongT5: Efficient Text-To-Text Transformer for Long Sequences
source.authors: Mandy Guo; Joshua Ainslie; David C. Uthus; Santiago Ontañón; Jianmo Ni; Yun-Hsuan Sung; Yinfei Yang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports downstream benchmark performance for LongT5 models at different parameter counts, providing evidence about performance changes with model size using downstream metrics rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit scaling laws, or test extrapolation from small runs or compute-optimal allocations. It cites Kaplan et al. in background. Rows below record the study's own comparisons of downstream scores across model sizes at matched input lengths.
record.test_reason: LongT5 is an architecture paper (TGlobal attention plus PSG pretraining). It cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation for scaling model size. It reports its own model's benchmark scores at three sizes (base ~220M, large ~770M, xl ~3B). It fits no scaling relation, measures no pretraining loss, and does not ask whether downstream gains are predictable from scale or loss. The size comparisons are its own method's performance, not a test of V6's predictability claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that TGlobal attention plus PSG pretraining lets T5 scale input length efficiently. Scaling input length and model size together gives state-of-the-art results on arXiv, PubMed, BigPatent, MediaSum and TriviaQA. They make no claims about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates LongT5 downstream task scores across model sizes and input lengths, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting power laws. It also changes the attention mechanism and pretraining objective.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with input length, attention mechanism, dataset, and model size. The authors note that NQ results include irregularities and are based on one run per configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Across three LongT5 sizes (220M, 770M, 3B), fine-tuned downstream scores generally rise with size at matched input length. Gains range from negligible (arXiv R-1 +0.07) to large (BigPatent R-1 +6.5). No fit is made and NQ results come from single runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In long-input encoder-decoder fine-tuning, larger models score higher, but the size gain varies widely by task.

record.problems: The study does not measure the loss or fit scaling relationships. It reports no uncertainty estimates for the extracted comparisons; the authors specifically state that NQ results are from one repetition per experiment and may contain noise.
record.rows_left_out: Other model sizes, input lengths, metrics, baselines, and task results in Tables 2, 4, 7, and 8 are not extracted. The rows retain representative matched-input-length comparisons across tasks and metrics; they do not represent a fitted or exhaustive scaling analysis.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss reported, no power-law fit.
No compute-optimal allocation; all models pretrained for a fixed 1M steps.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits for fine-tuning or other regimes.
Only three model sizes, no fit, no relation to pretraining loss, no predictability test.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V6 'supports' label are overturned. Size is used as a design lever, and the paper reports its own model's benchmark numbers without analysing predictability. Kaplan et al. appears only in the introduction.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute; power-law behavior.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their trends with compute.
Loss comparisons isolating depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The study compares downstream scores across some model sizes, but does not fit or evaluate a predictive relationship, test performance against pretraining loss, or establish predictability across orders of magnitude.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.
